phy_ocrb.5.0.summary: This topic covers the particle model concept of density and how to experimentally determine the density of regular solids, irregular solids, and liquids using precise laboratory equipment as required by PAG1. Students must master the density formula, standard units, and the practical techniques including balances, displacement cans, and measuring cylinders. Achieving a Grade 9 requires deep understanding of measurement uncertainties, meniscus reading, and why identical masses of different states of matter have vastly different volumes.

core.p: Density is a fundamental property of matter that describes how tightly packed the particles are within a given volume. It links mass and volume, determining whether an object will sink or float in a fluid.
bullets: Definition: Mass per unit volume of a substance.
Equation: Density equals mass divided by volume.
Symbol equation: rho = m / V
Standard SI units: kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³).
Alternative common units: grams per cubic centimetre (g/cm³).
Conversion rule: To convert g/cm³ to kg/m³, multiply by 1000.

callouts.p: Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance.
Always check whether the question asks for kg/m³ or g/cm³ before finishing your calculation.

core.p: The relationship between density (rho), mass (m), and volume (V) can be manipulated mathematically using a formula triangle. This ensures you can correctly rearrange the equation regardless of what the exam question asks you to find.
bullets: To find Density (rho): Cover rho, calculate mass divided by volume (m / V).
To find Mass (m): Cover m, calculate density multiplied by volume (rho x V).
To find Volume (V): Cover V, calculate mass divided by density (m / rho).
Ensure all quantities are in consistent units before performing calculations.
Mass is typically measured in grams (g) or kilograms (kg).
Volume is typically measured in cubic centimetres (cm³) or cubic metres (m³).

callouts.p: Write down the formula you are given, substitute known values, and then solve to avoid algebraic errors.

core.p: Accurate determination of density requires precise measurement of mass using an electronic balance. Proper calibration and technique eliminate systematic errors.
bullets: Equipment: Digital top-pan balance sensitive to at least 0.1 g or 0.01 g.
Step 1: Turn on the balance and ensure it reads zero ('tare' or 'zero' button).
Step 2: Place the object gently on the centre of the pan.
Step 3: Read and record the digital display once the reading stabilizes.
Zeroing with containers: If measuring powder or liquid, place the empty container on the pan first, press tare, then add the substance.
Avoid touching objects with bare hands after weighing if skin oils add measurable mass.

callouts.p: Always tare the balance with the measuring boat or cylinder on it before adding the substance to measure only the substance's mass.

core.p: Regular solids have uniform geometrical shapes such as cubes, cuboids, cylinders, or spheres. Their volumes can be found using direct linear measurements and standard mathematical formulas.
bullets: Equipment: Ruler, vernier callipers, or micrometre screw gauge for high precision.
Cuboid volume: Length multiplied by width multiplied by height (V = l x w x h).
Cylinder volume: Pi multiplied by radius squared multiplied by length (V = pi x r² x h).
Sphere volume: Four thirds multiplied by pi multiplied by radius cubed (V = 4/3 x pi x r³).
Take multiple measurements along different parts of the object to check for uniformity and calculate an average.
Convert all linear dimensions to metres (for kg/m³) or centimetres (for g/cm³) before calculating volume.

callouts.p: Vernier callipers reduce parallax and zero errors compared to standard plastic rulers.

core.p: Irregular solids do not have simple geometric dimensions, so direct measurement is impossible. Instead, the displacement method using a Eureka can (displacement can) is employed.
bullets: Equipment: Eureka can, measuring cylinder, electronic balance, water, paper towels.
Step 1: Fill the Eureka can with water until water just begins to drip out of the spout into a waste beaker.
Step 2: Place a clean, dry measuring cylinder directly beneath the spout to catch displaced water.
Step 3: Gently lower the irregular solid into the water using a fine thread until it is fully submerged.
Step 4: Collect all the displaced water in the measuring cylinder.
Step 5: Read the volume of displaced water at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus. The volume of the solid equals the volume of displaced water.

callouts.p: Ensure the water level is exactly at the bottom of the spout before starting, otherwise excess water will overflow prematurely.

core.h: 6. Measuring Volume and Density of Liquids (PAG1)
core.p: Determining the density of a liquid requires measuring the mass of a known volume of that liquid using a measuring cylinder and a balance.
bullets: Equipment: Electronic balance, measuring cylinder, liquid sample.
Step 1: Place an empty measuring cylinder on the electronic balance and record its mass (m1).
Step 2: Pour a known volume (V) of liquid (e.g., 50 cm³) into the measuring cylinder.
Step 3: Record the total mass of the cylinder and liquid together (m2).
Step 4: Calculate the mass of the liquid alone by subtracting m1 from m2 (m = m2 - m1).
Step 5: Calculate density using rho = mass / volume.

callouts.p: Repeat the procedure with increasing volumes of liquid (e.g., 20cm³, 40cm³, 60cm³) and plot a mass-volume graph. The gradient gives the density.

core.p: Liquids in narrow glass or plastic containers curve at the edges due to surface tension and adhesive forces with the container walls. This curve is called a meniscus.
bullets: Rule for water: Water forms a concave meniscus (curves downwards in the middle).
Reading technique: Always read the scale at eye level aligned with the **bottom of the meniscus**.
Parallax error: Looking from above or below introduces systematic errors, making volume readings too high or too low.
Ensure the measuring cylinder is placed on a completely flat, horizontal surface before taking readings.

callouts.p: Examiners frequently penalise students who fail to state that readings must be taken at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus.

core.p: Plotting experimental results on a graph provides a powerful way to determine density while reducing the impact of random experimental errors.
bullets: Independent variable (x-axis): Volume (cm³ or m³).
Dependent variable (y-axis): Mass (g or kg).
Line of best fit: Draw a straight line of best fit passing through or close to the origin (0,0).
Calculating gradient: Choose two points on the line far apart, calculate change in mass divided by change in volume (delta m / delta V).
Physical meaning: The gradient of a mass-volume graph represents the **density** of the substance.

callouts.p: Gradient = rise / run = mass / volume = density. A steeper gradient means a higher density.

core.p: An object's density relative to the fluid it is placed in determines whether it floats or sinks. This is governed by the principles of upthrust and weight.
bullets: General rule: An object will **float** in a fluid if its average density is **less** than the density of the fluid.
General rule: An object will **sink** in a fluid if its average density is **greater** than the density of the fluid.
Neutral buoyancy: If an object's density equals the fluid density, it will remain suspended at that depth.
Ice floats on liquid water because the crystalline structure of ice makes its density lower (approx. 917 kg/m³) than liquid water (1000 kg/m³).

callouts.p: An object floats when the upthrust acting on it equals its total weight.

core.h: 10. Precision, Accuracy, and Errors in PAG1
core.p: Top grade students understand the limitations of equipment and how random and systematic errors affect density determinations.
bullets: Random errors: Variations in reading measuring cylinders or slight mass fluctuations on balances. Reduced by repeating measurements and calculating a mean.
Systematic errors: Zero errors on electronic balances or miscalibrated measuring cylinders. Reduced by zeroing equipment before use.
Water retention: If an irregular solid absorbs water (e.g., porous rock), measured mass after immersion will be too high, leading to an artificially high calculated density.
Spillage: Splashing water out of a Eureka can before the object is submerged leads to incorrect volume displacement readings.

callouts.p: Be prepared in exams to evaluate experimental methods and suggest improvements to reduce percentage uncertainty.

analogy.p: Imagine a 100 square metre room filled with people. If the room contains 10 toddlers, they are spread out with low density (like gas particles). If the same room is packed with 500 adults standing shoulder-to-shoulder, the density is extremely high (like a solid). Where this analogy breaks down is that human beings can squeeze closer together or move around freely, whereas atoms and molecules in solids have fixed vibrational positions and strong intermolecular forces preventing easy compression.

The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg) or grams (g).
The amount of three-dimensional space an object occupies, measured in m³ or cm³.
A displacement can used to measure the volume of irregular solid objects.
The curved upper surface of a liquid in a tube or measuring cylinder.
An error in reading a scale caused by not viewing the marker directly at eye level.
The process where an immersed object pushes aside a volume of fluid equal to its own submerged volume.
A sensitive electronic instrument used to measure the mass of objects.
An object with uniform geometric dimensions allowing direct calculation of volume.
An object without simple geometric dimensions requiring water displacement to find volume.

mistakes.r: Density equals mass divided by volume (rho = m / V).

mistakes.w: Reading the top of the meniscus for liquid volume.
mistakes.r: Always read from the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to zero (tare) the balance before measuring.
mistakes.r: Always tare the balance with containers or weighing boats on the pan first.

mistakes.w: Units for density are kg/cm³.
mistakes.r: Standard SI units are kg/m³; laboratory units are usually g/cm³.

mistakes.w: Water level in a Eureka can should be below the spout.
mistakes.r: Water level must be exactly level with the bottom of the spout, with excess drained off.

mistakes.w: Mass changes depending on gravity.
mistakes.r: Mass is the amount of matter and stays constant; weight is the force due to gravity.

exam.q: State the equation linking density, mass, and volume.
model: density = mass / volume (or rho = m / V)
exam.tip: Learn standard symbols and word equations perfectly.

exam.q: Describe how to measure the volume of an irregular solid using a Eureka can.
model: Fill Eureka can with water until it drips out of the spout
Place a measuring cylinder under the spout
Lower the irregular solid fully into the water
Measure the volume of water collected in the measuring cylinder
exam.tip: List the steps in chronological order for full marks.

exam.q: A block of metal has a mass of 540 g and a volume of 200 cm³. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
model: rho = 2.7 g/cm³
exam.tip: Always state the formula, substitute numbers, and include correct units.

exam.q: Explain why reading a measuring cylinder from above causes an incorrect volume reading.
model: Causes a parallax error
Makes the measured volume appear higher than the true value
exam.tip: Mention both the name of the error and the direction of the inaccuracy.

exam.q: Convert a density of 2.7 g/cm³ into kg/m³.
model: Multiply by 1000
2700 kg/m³
exam.tip: Remember 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.

exam.q: Describe how to find the density of an unknown liquid using a measuring cylinder and balance.
model: Measure mass of empty measuring cylinder
Pour a known volume of liquid into the cylinder
Measure total mass and subtract empty cylinder mass
Divide mass of liquid by volume
exam.tip: Clearly show how the mass of the liquid alone is isolated.

exam.q: Explain why ice floats on water.
model: Ice has a lower density than liquid water
Objects with lower density than the fluid they are in will float
exam.tip: Reference relative densities, not just 'ice is lighter'.

exam.q: An irregular solid absorbs water during a displacement experiment. Explain how this affects the calculated density.
model: Water absorbed means less water is displaced into the measuring cylinder
Measured volume is too low
Calculated density will be too high
exam.tip: Trace the error through the formula: smaller volume denominator means larger density result.

exam.q: Describe how plotting a mass-volume graph helps determine density more accurately than a single measurement.
model: Allows a line of best fit to be drawn which reduces the effect of random errors
The gradient of the line gives the density
exam.tip: Always link graph features (gradient) to physical properties (density).

worked.q: A copper cylinder has a radius of 2.0 cm and a height of 10.0 cm. Its mass is 1115 g. Calculate the density of copper in g/cm³.
steps: Calculate the volume of the cylinder using V = pi x r² x h. V = 3.142 x (2.0)² x 10.0 = 125.68 cm³.
Use the density formula rho = mass / volume. rho = 1115 / 125.68.
Calculate final value: rho = 8.87 g/cm³.

worked.q: A student measures the mass of an empty beaker as 60.0 g. After adding 50 cm³ of oil, the total mass is 105.0 g. Calculate the density of the oil.
steps: Find the mass of the oil by subtracting beaker mass from total mass: m = 105.0 g - 60.0 g = 45.0 g.
Identify the volume of the oil: V = 50 cm³.
Calculate density: rho = 45.0 / 50 = 0.90 g/cm³.

phy_ocrb.5.1.summary: These top-tier revision notes cover specific heat capacity and the required practical (PAG5) for OCR GCSE Physics B (Twenty First Century Science). They provide a grade-9 level breakdown of thermal energy transfer, temperature changes, formula manipulations, experimental setups, control variables, and graphical analysis of heating curves.

core.p: Specific heat capacity is a fundamental thermal property that describes how much energy is required to change the temperature of a given substance. Different materials respond differently to heating because of their atomic structure and the strength of bonds between particles.
bullets: It is a measure of how resistant a material is to changes in temperature.
Materials with a high specific heat capacity store a large amount of thermal energy for every degree rise in temperature.
It depends entirely on the identity of the material and its mass.

callouts.p: The specific heat capacity of a substance is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 °C (or 1 K) without changing its state.

core.p: To calculate energy changes when a material is heated or cooled, we use the standard specific heat capacity equation. Every term in this equation has strict units that you must convert before substituting numbers into calculations.
bullets: Equation: E = m x c x Delta θ
E represents the thermal energy transferred in joules (J).
m represents the mass in kilograms (kg).
c represents the specific heat capacity in joules per kilogram degree Celsius (J/(kg°C)).
Delta θ represents the change in temperature in degrees Celsius (°C).

callouts.p: Always ensure mass is in kg and temperature change is in °C before calculating.

core.p: When you supply thermal energy to a substance, the internal energy of the system increases. This results in either an increase in the kinetic energy of the particles, leading to a temperature rise, or a change of state.
bullets: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles within the substance.
When Delta θ is positive, energy is being absorbed by the system.
When Delta θ is negative, energy is being dissipated or transferred to the surroundings as the object cools.

callouts.p: Always calculate Delta θ as Final Temperature minus Initial Temperature.

core.h: 4. Overview of PAG5: Investigating Specific Heat Capacity
core.p: Required Practical 5 (PAG5) involves experimentally determining the specific heat capacity of a solid material, such as an aluminium or copper block, or a liquid like water, using electrical heating equipment.
bullets: The aim is to measure how much electrical energy is transferred to a material and relate it to the resulting temperature rise.
You must measure the mass of the block using a digital balance before starting.
An electric immersion heater supplies thermal energy at a known rate.

callouts.p: Core equipment includes a metal block with holes for a heater and thermometer, a power supply, a joulemeter or ammeter/voltmeter/stopclock, insulation, and a pipette of oil.

core.p: Executing the experiment requires a strict step-by-step methodology to minimise systematic and random errors, ensuring your calculated specific heat capacity is as close to the accepted literature value as possible.
bullets: Measure and record the mass (m) of the metal block using a top-pan balance.
Place a small amount of thermal paste or oil into the thermometer hole to ensure good thermal contact between the block and the thermometer.
Record the initial temperature (θ1) of the block before turning on the power supply.
Turn on the power supply and start a stopclock simultaneously.
Record the voltage (V) and current (I) from the meters, or read the energy directly if using a joulemeter.

callouts.p: Always mention thermal paste or oil in exams; it removes air gaps that act as thermal insulators.

core.h: 6. Controlling Variables and Improving Thermal Contact
core.p: To obtain valid results in PAG5, you must carefully control variables that could allow thermal energy to escape to the surroundings, leading to systematic overestimation of the specific heat capacity.
bullets: Independent variable: The type of material or the amount of energy transferred.
Dependent variable: The temperature of the material.
Control variables: Mass of the material, starting temperature, and the surrounding room temperature.
Wrap the metal block in insulating lagging to minimise thermal energy losses to the surrounding air.

callouts.p: Failure to insulate the block causes heat loss to the room, meaning Delta θ is too small, so calculated c is too large.

core.p: When a joulemeter is not available, you must calculate the thermal energy supplied to the immersion heater using electrical measurements of potential difference, current, and time.
bullets: Equation for electrical work done / energy transferred: E = P x t
Electrical power P is calculated using: P = V x I
Combining these gives: E = V x I x t
V is potential difference in volts (V), I is current in amperes (A), and t is time in seconds (s).

callouts.p: Energy transferred electrically is the product of power and time, or current, potential difference, and time.

core.h: 8. Processing PAG5 Results and Plotting Graphs
core.p: Raw data collected from the experiment must be processed graphically to find the specific heat capacity accurately, accounting for systematic errors like initial warm-up time.
bullets: Calculate temperature change Delta θ for each time interval.
Plot a graph of work done / energy transferred (y-axis) against temperature change Delta θ (x-axis).
Draw a line of best fit, ignoring any initial non-linear warm-up anomalies.
The gradient of this linear graph represents m x c.

callouts.p: Gradient = Energy / Delta θ = m x c. Therefore, c = Gradient / mass.

core.h: 9. Comparing Specific Heat Capacities of Materials
core.p: Different substances have vastly different specific heat capacities due to the nature of their chemical bonds and intermolecular forces. Water has an unusually high specific heat capacity compared to metals.
bullets: Water has a specific heat capacity of approximately 4200 J/(kg°C), making it exceptional for storing thermal energy.
Copper has a much lower specific heat capacity (around 385 J/(kg°C)), meaning it heats up and cools down very rapidly.
High specific heat capacity materials make excellent thermal buffers and coolant fluids in engines and heating systems.

callouts.p: Water requires 4200 J to raise 1 kg by 1 °C, explaining why coastal areas have milder climates than inland areas.

core.p: Understanding specific heat capacity allows engineers and scientists to design efficient thermal systems, storage heaters, and cooling mechanisms for industrial and domestic applications.
bullets: Storage heaters use bricks with high specific heat capacities to store thermal energy overnight when electricity is cheaper, releasing it slowly during the day.
Car engine coolants use water mixed with additives to absorb massive amounts of thermal energy without boiling.
Cooking utensils made of aluminium or copper heat food quickly because of low specific heat capacity and high thermal conductivity.

callouts.p: Be prepared to apply SHC calculations to radiators, storage heaters, and geothermal energy systems.

analogy.t: The Sponge and Water Bucket Analogy
analogy.p: Imagine specific heat capacity as how sponge-like an object is for thermal energy. A high specific heat capacity material is like a giant, highly absorbent sponge: you can pour buckets of water (thermal energy) into it, but the water level (temperature) barely rises. A low specific heat capacity material is like a tiny sponge: just a few drops of water make it overflow instantly. Where the analogy breaks down: sponges hold physical liquid water inside pores, whereas materials store thermal energy as increased kinetic and potential energy of their microscopic particles.

terms.d: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C without changing state.
The total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles within a system.
The total energy stored inside a system by the particles that make up the system.
A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance.
A device used to measure the amount of electrical energy transferred directly in joules.
An electrical heating element submerged in a substance to transfer thermal energy.
Insulating material wrapped around an apparatus to reduce thermal energy transfer to the surroundings.
A substance applied between surfaces to eliminate air gaps and improve thermal contact.
The steepness of a graph line, calculated as change in y divided by change in x.
The rate at which energy is transferred or work is done, measured in watts (W).
The work done per unit charge between two points in a circuit, measured in volts (V).
The rate of flow of electrical charge, measured in amperes (A).

mistakes.w: Saying specific heat capacity is the energy to melt 1 kg of a substance.
mistakes.r: That is specific latent heat of fusion. Specific heat capacity involves temperature change, not state change.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to convert grams to kilograms when calculating energy.
mistakes.r: Always divide mass in grams by 1000 to get kilograms before using E = mcΔθ.

mistakes.w: Writing units as degrees Celsius per joule.
mistakes.r: The correct unit is joules per kilogram degree Celsius (J/(kg°C)).

mistakes.w: Confusing temperature with thermal energy.
mistakes.r: Temperature is average kinetic energy; thermal energy is total kinetic and potential energy.

mistakes.w: Stating that insulation stops heat from escaping completely.
mistakes.r: Insulation reduces the rate of thermal energy transfer, it does not stop it entirely.

mistakes.w: Calculating temperature change as initial minus final.
mistakes.r: Always use final temperature minus initial temperature (or magnitude of change).

mistakes.w: Ignoring electrical power equations when calculating energy supplied.
mistakes.r: Remember E = VIt when a joulemeter is not used in PAG5.

exam.q: Define the term 'specific heat capacity'.
model: The energy required (1)
to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C (1)
exam.tip: Learn this definition word for word as it is a frequent 2-mark recall question.

exam.q: A student investigates the specific heat capacity of an aluminium block of mass 2.0 kg. The electrical heater transfers 18,000 J of energy, causing the temperature to rise by 10 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium.
model: State equation: E = mcΔθ (1)
Substitute values: 18000 = 2.0 x c x 10 (1)
Calculate c: c = 900 J/(kg°C) (1)
exam.tip: Always show your working clearly, even for simple substitution questions.

exam.q: Explain why wrapping the metal block in insulating material improves the accuracy of the specific heat capacity experiment in PAG5.
model: Reduces thermal energy transfer to the surroundings (1)
Meaning more of the supplied electrical energy is used to heat the block, making Δθ more accurate (1)
exam.tip: Link the insulation to reduced heat loss and how that affects the measured temperature change.

exam.q: State two control variables a student must keep constant when comparing the specific heat capacities of two different metal blocks.
model: Mass of the metal blocks (1)
Initial temperature of the blocks (or room temperature / power supplied) (1)
exam.tip: Keep control variables specific: name the exact physical quantity to be kept the same.

exam.q: A block of copper has a mass of 1.5 kg and a specific heat capacity of 385 J/(kg°C). Calculate the thermal energy needed to increase its temperature from 20 °C to 70 °C.
model: Calculate Δθ = 70 - 20 = 50 °C (1)
Substitute into E = mcΔθ: E = 1.5 x 385 x 50 (1)
Calculate E = 28875 J (or 28900 J) (1)
exam.tip: Remember to calculate the temperature change first before multiplying by mass and SHC.

exam.q: Explain why thermal paste or oil is placed into the hole where the thermometer is inserted into the metal block.
model: Fills air gaps between the thermometer and the metal block (1)
Air is a poor thermal conductor, so oil improves thermal contact and ensures an accurate temperature reading (1)
exam.tip: Examiners always award marks for mentioning that air acts as an insulator.

exam.q: A 0.5 kg block of lead is supplied with 3250 J of energy. Its specific heat capacity is 130 J/(kg°C). Calculate the temperature rise.
model: Rearrange equation: Δθ = E / (mc) (1)
Substitute values: Δθ = 3250 / (0.5 x 130) (1)
Calculate Δθ = 50 °C (1)
exam.tip: Show rearrangement steps clearly if you need to find something other than energy.

exam.q: Describe how a student can use an ammeter, voltmeter, and stopclock to find the energy transferred by a heater during PAG5.
model: Multiply potential difference (V) by current (I) to find power (1)
Measure the time (t) the heater is switched on using a stopclock (1)
Calculate energy using E = VIt (1)
exam.tip: State all three measuring instruments and how their readings combine to give energy.

exam.q: Explain why water has a much higher specific heat capacity than metals.
model: Water molecules have strong hydrogen bonds between them (1)
More thermal energy is required to break or disrupt these bonds and increase particle kinetic energy (1)
exam.tip: Relate high SHC to intermolecular bonding at the particle level for higher tier credit.

worked.q: A student uses an immersion heater in a 1.0 kg aluminium block. The heater is connected to a 12 V power supply and draws a current of 2.0 A for 300 seconds. The initial temperature of the block is 20.0 °C and the final temperature is 28.0 °C. Calculate the experimental specific heat capacity of aluminium and suggest one reason why it differs from the accepted value of 900 J/(kg°C).
steps: Calculate energy transferred: E = V x I x t = 12 x 2.0 x 300 = 7200 J.
Calculate temperature change: Delta θ = 28.0 - 20.0 = 8.0 °C.
Rearrange specific heat capacity equation: c = E / (m x Delta θ).
Substitute values: c = 7200 / (1.0 x 8.0) = 900 J/(kg°C).

Reason for difference: Thermal energy escaped to the surroundings, meaning not all electrical energy heated the block (though in this idealised numbers case it matches exactly, real experiments yield higher calculated values due to heat loss).
worked.ans: Specific heat capacity = 900 J/(kg°C). Difference is caused by thermal energy loss to the surroundings.

worked.q: Calculate the final temperature of a 2.0 kg block of copper (specific heat capacity = 385 J/(kg°C)) starting at 15 °C when 77,000 J of thermal energy is supplied to it.
steps: Identify knowns: E = 77000 J, m = 2.0 kg, c = 385 J/(kg°C), initial temperature = 15 °C.
Rearrange equation for temperature change: Delta θ = E / (m x c).
Substitute values: Delta θ = 77000 / (2.0 x 385).
Calculate Delta θ: Delta θ = 77000 / 770 = 100 °C.
Calculate final temperature: Final Temperature = Initial Temperature + Delta θ = 15 + 100 = 115 °C.
worked.ans: The final temperature of the copper block is 115 °C.

phy_ocrb.5.3.summary: This comprehensive revision guide covers the particle model, density, changes of state, internal energy, and gas pressure for OCR GCSE Physics B (Twenty First Century Science). It explores how particles behave in solids, liquids, and gases, how energy changes during state transitions, and the microscopic origins of gas pressure. Mastering these concepts provides a rigorous framework for understanding thermal physics and the kinetic theory of matter at a Grade 9 level.

core.h: 1. States of Matter and the Particle Model
core.p: The particle model explains the physical properties of matter by assuming that all substances are made of very small particles (atoms, molecules, or ions). The arrangement, spacing, and movement of these particles determine whether a substance is a solid, a liquid, or a gas.
bullets: **Solids**: Particles are closely packed in a regular lattice structure, vibrating about fixed positions with strong inter-molecular forces.
**Liquids**: Particles are closely packed but arranged randomly and can slide past one another, maintaining a fixed volume.
**Gases**: Particles are far apart, move rapidly and randomly in all directions, and have very weak inter-molecular forces.
Density is generally highest in solids, lower in liquids, and lowest in gases, though water is an important exception due to its open crystalline structure when frozen.

head: State
Particle Spacing
Movement
Shape and Volume
rows: Move around, slide past each other
Takes shape of container, fixed volume

callouts.p: A model that describes matter as being made of particles constantly moving and interacting, used to explain the properties of solids, liquids, and gases.
Liquids and solids are virtually incompressible because their particles are already touching, whereas gases are easily compressed because of large empty spaces between particles.

core.p: Internal energy is the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles that make up a system. It is a fundamental concept in thermodynamics that determines the thermal state of matter.
bullets: **Kinetic Energy component**: Associated with the random motion of particles. Higher temperature means higher average kinetic energy.
**Potential Energy component**: Associated with the positions of particles and the inter-molecular forces between them.
Heating a system transfers energy into its thermal store, increasing the internal energy and raising the temperature or causing a change of state.
Internal energy does **not** equal heat; heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference.

callouts.p: The total energy stored inside a system by the particles that make up the system, consisting of the total kinetic energy and potential energy of the particles.
Never say 'molecules contain heat'. Molecules contain internal energy (kinetic and potential), while heat is energy transferred.

core.p: When a substance changes state, physical properties change, but its mass is conserved. Changes of state are physical processes, meaning no new substances are created and the process can be reversed.
bullets: **Melting**: Solid to liquid.
**Boiling / Evaporation**: Liquid to gas.
**Condensing**: Gas to liquid.
**Freezing**: Liquid to solid.
**Sublimation**: Solid directly to gas (e.g., solid carbon dioxide / dry ice).

callouts.p: During any change of state, mass is always conserved because the total number of particles remains exactly the same.
Always state that changes of state are physical changes, not chemical changes, when asked why mass is conserved.

core.h: 4. Temperature vs Potential Energy during State Changes
core.p: During a change of state, energy is supplied or removed, but the temperature of the substance remains constant. This is because the energy supplied is changing the potential energy of the particles rather than their kinetic energy.
bullets: When heating a solid, temperature rises as kinetic energy increases.
At the melting point, added energy breaks bonds between particles, increasing potential energy while temperature stays flat.
Once completely melted, adding more energy increases liquid particle kinetic energy and temperature rises again.
At the boiling point, energy is used to break remaining inter-molecular bonds completely to form a gas.

callouts.p: The energy needed for a substance to change state without changing its temperature.
Students often think temperature must always rise when heated. On a heating curve, flat horizontal sections represent changes of state where temperature is constant.

core.p: Gas pressure is caused by the random impact of gas molecules on the walls of a container. As gas particles move continuously, they collide with container surfaces, exerting a force perpendicular to the surface.
bullets: Each collision exerts a tiny force over the surface area.
Total pressure is the sum of all forces exerted by particle collisions per unit area.
Gas molecules have a range of speeds, but temperature is proportional to the average kinetic energy of the particles.
Absolute zero (0 K or -273 °C) is the temperature at which particles have minimum kinetic energy.

callouts.p: The force exerted per unit area by gas molecules colliding with the walls of their container.
Kelvin temperature is directly proportional to the average kinetic energy of gas molecules. To convert Celsius to Kelvin, add 273.

core.p: Gas pressure can be altered by changing the temperature, volume, or number of gas particles in a container. Each factor affects the frequency or force of particle collisions.
bullets: **Temperature increase**: Particles move faster, colliding with walls more frequently and with greater force, increasing pressure.
**Volume decrease**: Compressing a gas packs particles into a smaller space, causing more frequent collisions with walls, increasing pressure.
**Adding more gas**: Increasing the number of particles increases the number of collisions per second, increasing pressure if volume and temperature are constant.

callouts.p: Always mention both 'frequency of collisions' and 'force of collisions' when explaining changes in gas pressure due to temperature.
Decreasing container volume does not make particles move faster; it only increases collision frequency because they have less distance to travel between walls.

core.h: 7. Pressure and Volume Relationship (Boyle's Law - Triple)
core.p: For a fixed mass of gas at a constant temperature, the pressure and volume are inversely proportional. If the volume of a gas is halved, its pressure is doubled.
bullets: Equation: p * V = constant
Or: p1 * V1 = p2 * V2
p is pressure in Pascals (Pa) or atmospheres
V is volume in cubic metres (m³) or cm³
This relationship holds true because smaller volume means particles hit the walls more often.

callouts.p: The product of pressure and volume for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature is a constant: p * V = constant.
When two variables are inversely proportional, doubling one halves the other.

core.p: Doing work on a gas transfers energy to it, increasing its internal energy and usually resulting in an increase in temperature or pressure.
bullets: When you pump up a bicycle tyre quickly, you do work on the gas inside using a piston.
The force moving the piston transfers energy to the kinetic energy of the gas molecules.
This increases the internal energy of the gas, which is why the pump feels warm.
Refrigerators and heat pumps also rely on doing work on gases to transfer thermal energy.

callouts.p: Energy transferred to a gas when a force is applied to compress or expand it.
Relate bicycle pump heating directly to work done increasing the kinetic energy store of the gas particles.

analogy.p: Imagine a squash court filled with hundreds of people throwing tennis balls randomly against the walls. The impact of each ball represents a gas particle collision, and the collective buffeting felt by the walls represents gas pressure. If you heat the room up (give people energy), they throw balls harder and faster, increasing pressure. If you shrink the court size (decrease volume), people hit the walls much more frequently. This breaks down because real gas molecules do not get tired, their collisions are perfectly elastic (no kinetic energy is lost), and they experience quantum and electrostatic forces not felt by humans.

terms.d: A model of matter where substances are represented as tiny particles in constant motion.
The total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles in a system.
Energy transferred during a change of state without changing temperature.
Energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing temperature.
Force exerted per unit area by particles colliding with container walls.
The lowest possible temperature (-273 °C or 0 K) where particles have minimum kinetic energy.
For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure multiplied by volume is constant (p * V = constant).
Energy transferred when a force moves an object, such as compressing a gas.
The direct change of state from solid to gas without becoming a liquid.
An absolute temperature scale where 0 K is absolute zero and units equal Celsius degrees.
Explaining macroscopic properties of gases through microscopic particle motion.
Energy stored in an object due to the movement and position of its particles.

mistakes.w: Saying molecules expand when a solid melts or a gas heats up.
mistakes.r: The spaces between molecules or the volume of the substance changes, but the individual molecules do not expand.

mistakes.w: Stating that temperature increases during a change of state.
mistakes.r: Temperature remains constant during state changes because energy goes into changing potential energy, not kinetic energy.

mistakes.w: Explaining gas pressure just by saying 'particles hit each other'.
mistakes.r: Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of the container, not each other.

mistakes.w: Confusing heat and internal energy.
mistakes.r: Heat is energy in transit; internal energy is the energy stored within the system.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to convert Celsius to Kelvin in calculations.
mistakes.r: Always add 273 to Celsius temperatures when using gas laws involving absolute temperature.

mistakes.w: Stating particles stop moving at absolute zero.
mistakes.r: At absolute zero (0 K), particles have *minimum* kinetic energy, not zero kinetic energy.

mistakes.w: Saying compression heats a gas because friction between particles increases.
mistakes.r: Compression does work on the gas, transferring energy directly to the kinetic energy store of the particles.

exam.q: Explain why the temperature of a substance does not change while it is melting, even though energy is being supplied.
model: Energy supplied is used to overcome inter-molecular forces / break bonds
This increases the potential energy of the particles
Therefore, kinetic energy (and temperature) remains constant
exam.tip: Always link temperature to kinetic energy and state changes to potential energy.

exam.q: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in a gas compared to a solid.
model: Solid particles are close together in a regular lattice; gas particles are far apart randomly arranged
Solid particles vibrate about fixed positions; gas particles move rapidly and randomly in all directions
Solids have strong forces between particles; gases have very weak forces
Solids have a fixed shape/volume; gases fill their container
exam.tip: Make direct comparative statements covering arrangement, spacing, and movement.

exam.q: A fixed mass of gas has a volume of 0.04 m³ at a pressure of 150 kPa. Calculate the pressure if the volume is compressed to 0.015 m³ at constant temperature.
exam.tip: Check your units and rearrange the formula clearly before substituting numbers.

exam.q: Explain how pumping up a bicycle tyre causes the pump to become warm.
model: Work is done on the gas when pushing the piston
This transfers energy to the kinetic energy store of the gas particles
Increased kinetic energy raises the temperature of the gas and the pump
exam.tip: Use the phrase 'work done on the gas' to score the first marking point.

exam.q: Define internal energy.
model: The total kinetic energy and potential energy
of all the particles that make up the system
exam.tip: Learn this definition word for word as mark schemes are strict.

exam.q: Explain why decreasing the volume of a gas increases its pressure, assuming temperature is constant.
model: Particles are closer together in a smaller volume
This means they collide with the container walls more frequently
More frequent collisions result in a greater average force per unit area (pressure)
exam.tip: Focus on collision frequency, not particle speed, since temperature is constant.

exam.q: State what is meant by absolute zero in terms of particle motion.
model: The temperature at which particles have minimum
kinetic energy
exam.tip: Avoid saying 'zero kinetic energy' or 'particles stop moving' to prevent losing marks.

exam.q: Explain why mass is conserved during a change of state.
model: No particles are added or removed during the change
The total number of particles and their individual masses remain unchanged
exam.tip: Mention conservation of particle number for full credit.

exam.q: Describe the motion of particles in a liquid.
model: Particles move around / slide past each other
Motion is random
exam.tip: Keep descriptions concise and use standard OCR keywords.

worked.q: A gas cylinder has a volume of 0.012 m³ and contains gas at a pressure of 250,000 Pa. If the valve is opened and the gas expands into a larger container until its pressure drops to 100,000 Pa, calculate the new volume.
steps: Identify Boyle's Law equation: p1 * V1 = p2 * V2
List knowns: p1 = 250,000 Pa, V1 = 0.012 m³, p2 = 100,000 Pa
Rearrange for V2: V2 = (p1 * V1) / p2
Substitute values: V2 = (250000 * 0.012) / 100000
Calculate answer: V2 = 3000 / 100000 = 0.030 m³

worked.q: Explain the microscopic changes that occur when a gas in a sealed rigid container is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C.
steps: Convert temperatures to Kelvin or discuss temperature increase: Temperature increase means higher average kinetic energy of gas particles.
Particle speed: Particles move faster on average.
Collision frequency: Particles hit the container walls more frequently.
Collision force: Because they are moving faster, each collision exerts a greater force.
Conclusion: Increased frequency and force of collisions lead to a higher overall gas pressure.
worked.ans: Pressure increases due to faster particles colliding more frequently and with greater force against the container walls.

phy_ocrb.5.4.summary: This topic covers how applied forces cause solid objects to deform, distinguishing clearly between elastic deformation where an object returns to its original shape and plastic deformation where it suffers permanent structural change. Students must understand the physical mechanisms behind stretching, compression, and bending, and analyse force-extension behaviour including the limit of proportionality. Mastery of these concepts is essential for explaining material properties and evaluating mechanical safety under load.

core.h: Introduction to Deformation and Applied Forces
core.p: When a system of forces is applied to a stationary solid object, it does not simply accelerate as a whole; instead, the internal forces between its constituent particles react, causing the object to change its shape or size. This change is known as deformation. Depending on the magnitude of the force and the nature of the material, this deformation can be temporary or permanent.
bullets: A single force alone cannot deform an object in equilibrium; it requires a pair of balanced, opposite forces (or multiple forces) acting in different directions to stretch, compress, bend, or twist it.
Stretching forces act outwards to increase the length of an object.
Compressive forces act inwards to decrease the length or volume of an object.
Internal molecular and atomic bonds resist these applied forces, creating a restoring internal force.

callouts.p: A change in shape or size of an object brought about by the action of forces.
To deform an object without accelerating its centre of mass, the net force acting on the object must be zero.

fig.cap: Figure 1: Opposing forces causing stretching and compression of a solid bar.

core.p: Elastic deformation occurs when an object changes shape under the action of applied forces, but completely returns to its original dimensions and shape once those forces are removed. At the atomic level, the atoms are slightly displaced from their equilibrium positions, stretching or compressing the interatomic bonds like tiny springs, but they do not break or slide past each other.
bullets: The deformation is fully reversible upon unloading.
All work done in elastically deforming the object is stored as elastic potential energy within the material.
No permanent atomic rearrangement takes place.
Examples include stretching a rubber band within its limit or compressing a steel coil spring gently.

callouts.p: Deformation where the object returns to its original shape and size when the applied forces are removed.
Always state that the object returns to its original shape 'when the load is removed' to secure full credit.

core.p: Plastic deformation occurs when an object is subjected to forces so large that it is permanently deformed and does not return to its original shape when the forces are removed. Beyond a certain threshold of stress, the atomic planes within the crystalline structure of the material permanently slip past one another, resulting in permanent structural rearrangement.
bullets: The deformation is irreversible once the load is removed.
Some of the work done on the material is dissipated as thermal energy due to internal friction.
The object retains a permanent extension, bending, or shape change.
Common examples include bending a paperclip back and forth until it snaps or crushing a metal car frame in a collision.

callouts.p: Deformation resulting in a permanent change of shape that remains after the applied forces are removed.
Do not confuse plastic deformation with plastics (polymers); any material, including steel and copper, can undergo plastic deformation.

core.p: Distinguishing between elastic and plastic behaviour is crucial for structural engineering and material selection. Materials chosen for bridges must remain strictly elastic under normal loads, whereas materials used in car crumple zones are designed to undergo plastic deformation to absorb kinetic energy during a crash.
bullets: Elastic range occurs at lower applied loads.
Plastic range occurs beyond the elastic limit.
Energy is conserved and fully recoverable in elastic deformation.
Energy is partly dissipated and unrecoverable in plastic deformation.

core.h: The Limit of Proportionality and Hooke's Law
core.p: For many elastic materials, such as metal springs and wires, the extension produced is directly proportional to the applied force, provided the deformation does not exceed the limit of proportionality. This linear relationship is known as **Hooke's Law**.
bullets: Described mathematically by the equation F = kx, where F is force, k is the spring constant, and x is the extension.
The limit of proportionality is the point beyond which the force-extension graph is no longer a straight line.
Up to this limit, doubling the force doubles the extension.
Beyond this point, the material still exhibits elastic behaviour up to the elastic limit, but the relationship ceases to be linear.

callouts.p: The point up to which the extension of an object is directly proportional to the applied force.
The straight-line section of a force-extension graph represents obedience to Hooke's Law.

core.p: Plotting force on the vertical axis against extension on the horizontal axis yields crucial information about a material's mechanical properties. The gradient of the linear region gives the spring constant k.
bullets: A steeper straight-line gradient indicates a stiffer material with a larger spring constant k.
The area underneath the force-extension graph represents the work done in deforming the object.
If the deformation is elastic, this area equals the elastic potential energy stored in the object.
If plastic deformation occurs, the loading and unloading curves form a hysteresis loop, where the enclosed area represents thermal energy dissipated.

callouts.p: Remember that k = change in force / change in extension. Ensure you only use the linear portion of the graph for this calculation.

core.p: When a spring or elastic band is stretched within its limit of proportionality, work is done on it by the applied forces. This work is stored within the material as elastic potential energy (E_e).
bullets: Calculated using the formula: E_e = 0.5 * k * x^2, where k is the spring constant and x is the extension.
Alternatively, since work done is the area under the force-extension graph, E_e = 0.5 * F * x.
Doubling the extension quadruples the stored elastic potential energy due to the squared term.
Energy is fully recovered when the spring returns to its unstretched state.

callouts.p: Energy stored in an object as a result of deformation of its elastic structure.

core.p: Materials respond very differently when subjected to forces that push them towards and beyond their elastic limits. Engineers classify materials primarily as ductile or brittle based on their plastic deformation behaviour.
bullets: Ductile materials undergo significant plastic deformation before breaking, allowing them to be drawn into wires (e.g., copper, mild steel).
Brittle materials show very little or no plastic deformation before fracturing; they snap suddenly when stressed beyond their elastic limit (e.g., glass, cast iron, ceramics).
Stress-strain graphs for brittle materials terminate abruptly at the fracture point without a plastic flow region.
Ductile materials exhibit a yield point where plastic deformation increases rapidly with little increase in force.

callouts.p: Brittle materials are strong under compression but weak under tension because tiny surface cracks propagate rapidly under tensile stress.

core.p: The OCR specification requires students to investigate the relationship between force and extension for a spring. This practical forms a core component of experimental physics skills assessed in examination papers.
bullets: Apparatus: Spring suspended from a clamp stand, metre ruler clamped vertically alongside, mass hanger and slotted masses, pointer indicator.

Method: Measure the initial unstretched length of the spring using the pointer and ruler. Add a known mass (e.g., 100g / 1.0N), record the new position, and calculate the extension (stretched length minus original length).
Repeat for incremental mass additions up to a maximum safe limit.
Plot a graph of force (y-axis) against extension (x-axis) to identify the limit of proportionality.

callouts.p: Always read the metre ruler at eye level perpendicular to the pointer scale to avoid parallax errors.

core.p: Achieving accurate and reliable results in the force-extension practical requires careful management of experimental uncertainties and safety precautions.
bullets: Ensure the metre ruler is strictly vertical using a set square or plumb line so that extension measurements are horizontal-free.
Use a magnifying marker or thin pointer attached to the bottom of the spring to improve reading precision against the ruler scale.
Check that the spring does not exceed its elastic limit during data collection; unload and check that it returns to zero original length.
Safety precaution: Wear safety goggles and place a mat or sand bucket beneath hanging masses to protect feet in case the spring snaps.

callouts.p: Take repeat measurements of extension for each mass load and calculate a mean to reduce random error.

core.h: Real-World Applications of Elastic and Plastic Deformation
core.p: Understanding deformation allows engineers to design safer and more efficient structures and devices across various industries.
bullets: Vehicle Crumple Zones: Designed to crumple and undergo plastic deformation during a collision, increasing impact duration and reducing peak deceleration forces on passengers.
Arch Bridges and Concrete Beams: Steel reinforcement bars embedded in concrete provide tensile strength while concrete handles compression.
Sports Equipment: Pole vault poles store elastic potential energy efficiently during bending and release it to lift the athlete over the bar.
Safety Harnesses and Bungee Cords: Incorporate elastic webbing that stretches gradually to reduce sudden jerk forces on the human body.

analogy.p: Imagine a tightly packed group of people standing in a room representing atoms in a solid. If people gently nudge each other and step back to their exact spots when the push stops, that is elastic deformation. If someone is shoved so hard that they stumble forward, lose their footing, and permanently end up in a new spot in the room, that is plastic deformation. Where this breaks down is that people make active choices, whereas atoms respond purely according to electrostatic forces and quantum mechanical bonding potentials.

terms.d: A change in the shape or size of an object caused by the application of external forces.
Deformation where the object returns to its original shape and size when the applied forces are removed.
Deformation that results in a permanent, irreversible change of shape after the forces are removed.
The point up to which the extension of an object is directly proportional to the applied force.
The extension of an elastic object is directly proportional to the force applied, up to the limit of proportionality (F = kx).
A measure of the stiffness of a spring, defined as force per unit extension (k = F/x).
Energy stored within a deformed elastic object, calculated as E_e = 0.5 * k * x^2.
A material that undergoes substantial plastic deformation before fracturing.
A material that breaks with little or no plastic deformation when subjected to stress.
The maximum stress or force that can be applied without causing permanent deformation.
Energy transferred when a force moves an object, represented by the area under a force-extension graph.
An error in reading a scale caused by viewing the pointer or marker from an angle rather than perpendicularly.

mistakes.w: Stating that elastic objects never change shape permanently.
mistakes.r: They do change shape while the force is applied, but they return to their original shape when the force is removed.

mistakes.w: Confusing elastic limit with limit of proportionality.
mistakes.r: The limit of proportionality is where the graph stops being a straight line; the elastic limit is where permanent deformation begins (often very close to each other, but distinct terms).

mistakes.w: Writing that plastic deformation only happens to plastic materials like polythene.
mistakes.r: Plastic deformation refers to permanent structural change in any material, including metals like steel and copper.

mistakes.w: Forgetting units when calculating the spring constant.
mistakes.r: Spring constant k is measured in newtons per metre (N/m).

mistakes.w: Saying extension is the final length of the spring.
mistakes.r: Extension is the increase in length from the original unstretched length (x = l - l_0).

mistakes.w: Using the total length instead of extension in E_e = 0.5 k x^2.
mistakes.r: The variable x represents extension, never the total length of the spring.

mistakes.w: Assuming brittle materials cannot be strong.
mistakes.r: Brittle materials like high-grade concrete or glass can withstand massive compressive forces, but fail easily under tension.

Returns to its original shape and size when the forces are removed

Plastic deformation results in permanent/irreversible change of shape
In elastic deformation, atomic bonds stretch but do not break permanently
In plastic deformation, atomic planes slide past each other permanently
exam.tip: Structure your answer by defining both terms clearly and contrasting their reversibility.

model: Extension is directly proportional to the applied force up to the limit of proportionality
exam.tip: Mentioning 'directly proportional' and 'limit of proportionality' is essential.

model: F = k * x
exam.tip: Show substitution and include the correct unit (N) in your final answer.

Measure initial unstretched length of the spring
Add known mass (e.g. 100g / 1N) and measure new position
Subtract initial length from new length to find extension
Repeat for increasing mass values and record results
Ensure ruler is vertical and read scale at eye level to prevent parallax error
exam.tip: Cover apparatus, independent/dependent variables, measurement technique, and safety/accuracy precautions for full marks.

model: The point beyond which force and extension are no longer directly proportional
Represented on the graph where the straight line starts to curve
exam.tip: Reference both the proportionality aspect and the graphical appearance.

exam.tip: Remember to square the extension value before multiplying by k and 0.5.

exam.q: Explain why glass is classified as a brittle material rather than a ductile material.
model: It breaks or fractures with little or no plastic deformation
It snaps suddenly when stressed beyond its elastic limit without warning
exam.tip: Focus on the lack of plastic flow prior to failure.

model: The area underneath the force-extension graph
exam.tip: Area under the curve/line is always work done in this context.

exam.q: A car crumple zone undergoes plastic deformation during a crash. Explain why this is desirable for passenger safety.
model: Plastic deformation absorbs kinetic energy of the car
Increases the duration of the impact collision
Reduces the peak deceleration force experienced by passengers
exam.tip: Link energy absorption and increased impact time to reduced forces on passengers.

worked.q: A spring has an unstretched length of 0.15 m. When a force of 6.0 N is applied, its total length becomes 0.25 m. Assuming the limit of proportionality is not exceeded, calculate: (a) the extension of the spring, (b) the spring constant k, and (c) the elastic potential energy stored.
steps: Step 1: Calculate extension x = total length - original length. x = 0.25 m - 0.15 m = 0.10 m.
Step 2: Rearrange Hooke's Law F = kx to find k = F / x. k = 6.0 N / 0.10 m = 60 N/m.
Step 3: Calculate elastic potential energy using E_e = 0.5 * k * x^2. E_e = 0.5 * 60 * (0.10)^2 = 0.5 * 60 * 0.01 = 0.30 J.
worked.ans: (a) Extension = 0.10 m, (b) Spring constant k = 60 N/m, (c) Elastic potential energy = 0.30 J.

worked.q: During a materials testing experiment, a metal wire of initial length 1.20 m is subjected to a tensile force. A force-extension graph shows that at a force of 45 N, the wire has extended by 0.008 m. Calculate the spring constant of the wire and determine the work done in stretching the wire to this point.
steps: Step 1: Identify values: F = 45 N, x = 0.008 m.
Step 2: Calculate spring constant k = F / x = 45 / 0.008 = 5625 N/m.
Step 3: Calculate work done (energy stored) assuming elastic behaviour: Work = 0.5 * F * x = 0.5 * 45 * 0.008 = 0.18 J.
worked.ans: Spring constant = 5625 N/m, Work done = 0.18 J.

phy_ocrb.5.5.summary: This topic covers how springs and elastic materials respond to applied forces, focusing on the linear relationship between force and extension described by Hooke's Law. Students must master calculating force, spring constant, and extension, as well as determining the work done and elastic potential energy stored from force-extension graphs. Additionally, complete mastery of Required Practical 2 (PAG2) is essential for achieving a grade 9 in OCR Physics B.

core.h: Hooke's Law and the Linear Force-Extension Relationship
core.p: When a tensile force is applied to a spring, it stretches. For most elastic materials, provided the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded, the extension of the object is directly proportional to the force applied.
bullets: Direct proportionality means if you double the stretching force, the extension doubles.
The relationship is expressed mathematically as F = kx.
F represents the force applied in Newtons (N).
k represents the spring constant in Newtons per metre (N/m).
x represents the extension in metres (m).

callouts.p: The extension of an elastic object is directly proportional to the force applied, up to the limit of proportionality.
Always use extension (x = current length - original length), never the total stretched length, in F = kx calculations.

fig.cap: Figure 1: Force against extension graph showing the linear region governed by Hooke's Law up to the limit of proportionality.

core.p: The spring constant is a measure of the stiffness of a spring. A higher spring constant means a stiffer spring that requires a greater force to produce a given extension.
bullets: Units of the spring constant are Newtons per metre (N/m).
Rearranging F = kx gives k = F / x.
It can be found graphically by calculating the gradient of a linear force-extension graph.
Different materials and geometries result in different spring constants.
Stiffer springs have steeper gradients on force-extension axes.

callouts.p: On a force-extension graph with force on the y-axis and extension on the x-axis, the gradient equals the spring constant k.

core.p: OCR requires students to carry out an experiment to investigate the relationship between force and extension for a spring using a clamp stand, masses, a ruler, and a pointer.
bullets: Hang a spring from a secure clamp stand and attach a metre ruler vertically next to it.
Attach a pointer (like a bent paperclip) to the bottom of the spring to read exact measurements and avoid parallax error.
Record the initial un-stretched length of the spring at zero added force.
Add known weights (e.g., 1.0 N increments) successively and record the new position of the pointer.
Calculate extension for each mass by subtracting the original length from the stretched length.

callouts.p: Position your eyes level with the marker on the metre ruler when taking readings to ensure high accuracy.

core.h: PAG2 Data Analysis and Error Reduction
core.p: To achieve top marks in exam questions based on PAG2, you must know how to process data safely and accurately, including identifying anomalous results and calculating means.
bullets: Repeat measurements for each mass at least three times and calculate a mean extension.
Plot a graph of force (y-axis) against extension (x-axis).
Draw a line of best fit through the linear points, ignoring anomalies.
Ensure safety precautions are met: wear safety goggles and place a mat underneath hanging masses in case the spring snaps or masses fall.
Check if the line passes through the origin; if not, there may be a zero error in your length measurements.

callouts.p: Never stand directly beneath hanging heavy masses during a spring stretching experiment.

core.p: Deformation can be elastic or plastic depending on whether the material returns to its original shape when the stretching force is removed.
bullets: Elastic deformation: The object returns to its original size and length when the force is removed.
Plastic deformation: The object is permanently stretched and does not return to its original length when the force is removed.
The elastic limit marks the boundary between elastic and plastic behaviour.
Beyond the limit of proportionality, Hooke's Law no longer applies and the graph curves.
Internal bonds and atomic structures are permanently rearranged during plastic deformation.

callouts.p: Deformation where the object regains its original shape and dimensions completely once the applied force is removed.

core.h: Work Done in Stretching a Spring
core.p: When a force stretches or compresses a spring, work is done on the spring. This work is transferred to the spring as stored energy.
bullets: Work done is defined as energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance.
Work done (Joules) = Force (Newtons) * distance/extension (metres).
In the linear region, the force is not constant; it increases linearly from zero to a maximum value F.
Therefore, the work done to stretch a spring is calculated using the average force.
Work done = 0.5 * F * x.

callouts.p: Work done = 0.5 * F * x, which equals the area under the force-extension graph.

core.p: The work done in stretching a spring is stored inside the spring as elastic potential energy (Ee), provided the elastic limit is not exceeded.
bullets: Elastic potential energy is measured in Joules (J).
By substituting F = kx into the work done equation (0.5 * F * x), we derive the energy equation.
Doubling the extension quadruples the stored elastic potential energy because extension is squared.
If the spring undergoes plastic deformation, some energy is dissipated as thermal energy and is permanently lost.

callouts.p: Energy stored in an elastic object as a result of deforming it.

core.p: Real materials often depart from Hooke's law when loaded heavily. Understanding non-linear regions is crucial for top-tier exam performance.
bullets: The initial straight section follows Hooke's Law (F = kx).
The point where the graph starts to bend is the limit of proportionality.
Beyond this point, equal increments of force produce larger increments of extension.
To find the work done in non-linear regions, you must count squares under the graph or approximate triangles and rectangles.
Unloading a plastically deformed spring results in a hysteresis loop where the return path differs from the loading path.

callouts.p: Never use Ee = 0.5kx^2 when the spring is in its non-linear or plastically deformed region; you must find the area under the curve.

core.h: Combining Springs (Series and Parallel - Extension & Challenge)
core.p: While standard GCSE syllabi focus on single springs, extending knowledge to combinations tests deep structural understanding of spring constants.
bullets: Springs in parallel share the total load, reducing the extension for a given total force.
For two identical springs in parallel, the effective spring constant is doubled (k_total = 2k).
Springs in series experience the same full load individually, so their extensions add up.
For two identical springs in series, the effective spring constant is halved (k_total = k / 2).
Understanding this links the microscopic arrangement of bonds to macroscopic stiffness.

callouts.p: Parallel springs are stiffer (higher k); series springs are stretchier (lower k).

core.p: Success in quantitative spring calculations requires disciplined working out, correct unit conversions, and formula selection.
bullets: Always check units: convert centimetres (cm) to metres (m) by dividing by 100.
Ensure grams (g) of mass are converted to Newtons of force by dividing by 100 kg to g conversion, then multiplying by gravitational field strength (W = mg, typically g = 9.8 or 10 N/kg).
State the formula clearly before substituting numbers.
Include correct units in your final answer (e.g., N/m for k, J for energy, N for force).
Double-check whether the question asks for extension or total length.

callouts.p: Forgetting to convert cm to m is the most common cause of losing marks in F = kx calculations.

analogy.p: Imagine pulling a resistance exercise band. A light pull stretches it a little bit; double the pull and it stretches twice as far (Hooke's Law). The resistance you feel represents the spring constant. However, if you pull too hard, the band snaps or stays permanently stretched out of shape (plastic deformation and limit of proportionality). Where the analogy breaks down is that rubber bands actually exhibit non-linear stretching and heating effects much faster than precision steel laboratory springs.

mistakes.w: Stating that force is inversely proportional to extension.
mistakes.r: Force is directly proportional to extension within the elastic limit.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to convert centimeters to meters when calculating spring constant.
mistakes.r: Always convert cm to m (divide by 100) so units match N/m.

mistakes.w: Saying plastic deformation means the spring breaks.
mistakes.r: Plastic deformation means it is permanently stretched, not necessarily broken.

mistakes.w: Using Ee = 0.5kx^2 when the spring is stretched beyond the limit of proportionality.
mistakes.r: That equation only applies where Hooke's law holds true; otherwise, calculate the area under the non-linear graph.

mistakes.w: Believing the spring constant has units of Newtons (N).
mistakes.r: The spring constant has units of Newtons per metre (N/m).

mistakes.w: Measuring the bottom of the hanging mass instead of the pointer position.
mistakes.r: Use a fixed pointer attached directly to the base of the spring to measure extension accurately against the ruler.

In plastic deformation, the object is permanently stretched
It does not return to its original length once the force is removed
exam.tip: Use clear comparative language for both terms.

exam.q: Describe how you would carry out Required Practical 2 to determine the spring constant of a spring safely.
model: Set up a clamp stand with a hanging spring and vertical metre ruler next to it
Attach a pointer to the bottom of the spring and record the initial length/zero reading
Add known masses (e.g. 100 g / 1 N increments) to the spring

exam.tip: Include apparatus, method, measurements taken, safety precautions, and data analysis.

exam.tip: Remember to square the extension before multiplying by 0.5 and k.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by the limit of proportionality on a force-extension graph.
model: It is the point where the graph stops being a straight line
Force is no longer directly proportional to extension beyond this point
