exam.q: A student measures the un-stretched length of a spring as 15.0 cm. When a 4.0 N force is applied, the total length becomes 23.0 cm. Calculate the spring constant k.
model: Calculate extension x = 23.0 cm - 15.0 cm = 8.0 cm
Convert extension to metres: 8.0 / 100 = 0.08 m
Rearrange k = F / x
exam.tip: Watch out for total length vs extension and convert cm to m.

exam.q: Sketch a force-extension graph for a metal spring that has been stretched beyond its elastic limit.
model: Linear region starting at the origin representing Hooke's Law
A clear point indicating the limit of proportionality where the line curves
A non-linear region continuing upwards with a decreasing gradient or flattening curve
exam.tip: Ensure axes are labelled Force and Extension.

exam.q: Explain how the work done in stretching a spring can be determined from a force-extension graph.
model: Work done is equal to the area under the force-extension graph
Calculate the area of the triangle (0.5 * base * height) for the linear region
exam.tip: Link energy transferred to graphical area.

worked.q: A spring has a spring constant of 80 N/m. It is stretched by 12 cm within its elastic limit. Calculate the work done in stretching the spring.
steps: Identify given values: k = 80 N/m, extension x = 12 cm.
Convert extension to metres: x = 12 / 100 = 0.12 m.
Calculate force using F = kx: F = 80 * 0.12 = 9.6 N.
Calculate work done using Work Done = 0.5 * F * x: Work Done = 0.5 * 9.6 * 0.12 = 0.576 J.

worked.q: A spring is stretched with a force of 15 N. Its original length is 10.0 cm and its stretched length is 18.5 cm. Calculate the spring constant k and the elastic potential energy stored.
steps: Find extension x = 18.5 cm - 10.0 cm = 8.5 cm = 0.085 m.
Calculate spring constant k = F / x = 15 / 0.085 = 176.47 N/m.
Calculate elastic potential energy Ee = 0.5 * F * x = 0.5 * 15 * 0.085 = 0.6375 J.

phy_ocrb.5.8.summary: The solar system consists of the Sun and various orbiting bodies, including planets, dwarf planets, asteroids, and comets, held together by gravitational forces. Orbits of planets and comets are elliptical rather than perfect circles, with orbital speed changing depending on distance from the Sun. For stable circular orbits, a change in speed requires a corresponding change in orbital radius to maintain a constant gravitational force balance.

core.p: Our solar system is a gravitationally bound system containing one central star, the Sun, along with eight planets, their natural satellites, dwarf planets, asteroids, and comets. Everything in the solar system orbits the Sun or orbits objects within the system.
bullets: Contains eight planets divided into inner terrestrial planets and outer gas giants.
Dwarf planets like Pluto share orbits with other bodies and are smaller than major planets.
Asteroids are rocky bodies primarily found in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
Comets are icy bodies with highly elliptical orbits originating from the outer solar system.

callouts.p: The Sun and all the objects bound to it by gravity, including planets, moons, dwarf planets, asteroids, and comets.
Inner planets are rocky and dense; outer planets are large gas and ice giants.

core.p: Gravity is the universal force of attraction between all matter. In the solar system, the massive Sun exerts a strong gravitational force that pulls inwards on planets, keeping them bound in orbital motion.
bullets: Gravitational field strength depends on the mass of the body and the distance from it.
The force of gravity acts towards the centre of the massive body.
Without gravity, a planet would move off in a straight line at constant velocity due to inertia.
The combination of forward velocity and the central gravitational pull results in a curved orbital path.

callouts.p: The gravitational force provides the centripetal force required to keep objects moving in a curved path.
Gravity acts as an attractive force between masses, never a repulsive force.

core.p: All planets orbit the Sun in nearly circular paths, though strictly speaking, they are slightly elliptical with the Sun located at one focus. The plane of the planets' orbits is roughly aligned.
bullets: All planets orbit in the same direction (counter-clockwise when viewed from above the Sun's north pole).
Inner planets have shorter orbital radii and shorter orbital periods (years).
Outer planets travel much larger distances and take many Earth years to complete one orbit.
Orbital speed of a planet depends on its distance from the Sun.

callouts.p: The time taken for a body to complete one full orbit around another body.
Closer planets travel faster because the gravitational pull is stronger.

core.p: Comets have very different orbital characteristics compared to planets. Their orbits are highly elliptical (elongated) and eccentric, taking them from the inner solar system far out past Pluto.
bullets: Comets spend most of their time far from the Sun in the outer reaches of the solar system.
As a comet approaches the Sun, gravitational force increases rapidly.
The comet speeds up significantly as it slingshots around the inner solar system.
Comet tails always point away from the Sun due to solar wind and radiation pressure.

callouts.p: An oval-shaped curve where the sum of the distances from two focal points is constant.
Comets travel fastest when closest to the Sun (perihelion) and slowest when furthest away (aphelion).

core.p: For an object in a stable circular orbit, the gravitational force acting on the body supplies the centripetal force. This means the speed of the orbit is directly linked to the radius of the orbit.
bullets: If the orbital radius changes, the orbital speed must also change to maintain a stable orbit.
A smaller orbital radius means a stronger gravitational force.
To prevent falling into the Sun, a smaller radius requires a higher orbital speed.
If speed decreases at a given radius, the object will spiral inwards towards the massive body.

callouts.p: An orbit where the gravitational force constantly provides the correct centripetal force for a constant radius and speed.
Smaller radius = faster speed. Larger radius = slower speed.

core.p: The strength of the gravitational force between two objects decreases as the distance between their centres increases. This inverse-square relationship dictates how satellites and planets behave at different distances.
bullets: Halving the distance between a planet and the Sun quadruples the gravitational force.
To balance this increased pull, the planet's orbital speed must increase.
Satellites orbiting Earth follow the same rule: low Earth orbits require much higher speeds than geostationary orbits.
Geostationary satellites orbit at a much greater distance and take 24 hours to match Earth's rotation.

callouts.p: Satellites with an orbital period of exactly 24 hours, remaining above the same point on Earth's equator.

core.p: A satellite is any object that orbits a larger body. Satellites can be natural, such as moons orbiting planets, or artificial, launched by humans for communication, weather monitoring, and science.
bullets: Earth has one natural satellite: the Moon.
Moons are kept in orbit by the gravitational pull of the planet they circle.
Artificial satellites are placed at various heights depending on their function.
Communications satellites often use geostationary orbits high above the equator.

callouts.p: An object that orbits a larger celestial body.
Do not confuse orbital period with rotational period (day length) of the planet itself.

core.p: The speed of an object in a circular orbit can be calculated using the orbital radius and the time taken for one complete orbit.
bullets: The distance travelled in one circular orbit is the circumference of the orbit: distance = 2 x pi x r.
Orbital speed v is calculated using the equation: v = (2 x pi x r) / T.
r is the orbital radius measured from the centre of the central body to the orbiting body in metres.
T is the orbital period in seconds.

callouts.p: v = 2 x pi x r / T, where v is speed, r is radius, and T is period.
Always convert orbital period into seconds and radius into metres before calculating speed.

core.p: When solving problems involving orbital speed, pay careful attention to whether the radius is given directly or if you need to add the radius of the central body to the altitude.
bullets: If a satellite orbits at an altitude h above a planet of radius R, the orbital radius r = R + h.
Pi (pi) should be used as approximately 3.14 or using the calculator button.
Rearranging the formula allows calculation of period T if speed and radius are known: T = (2 x pi x r) / v.
Ensure answers are given to appropriate significant figures.

callouts.p: Orbital radius r must be measured from the centre of mass, not from the surface of the planet.

core.p: As a body moves along an elliptical orbit, its gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy constantly interchange while total mechanical energy is conserved.
bullets: When a comet moves closer to the Sun, its gravitational potential energy decreases.
Because total energy is conserved, its kinetic energy increases, so it speeds up.
At its furthest point from the Sun (aphelion), gravitational potential energy is at its maximum and kinetic energy is at its minimum.
This energy conservation explains why speeds vary continuously in non-circular orbits.

callouts.p: Total energy (kinetic + gravitational potential) remains constant throughout an eccentric orbit.

core.p: Maintaining a stable orbit requires a precise balance between speed, mass, and gravitational pull. Any perturbation can alter the orbit's characteristics.
bullets: If a satellite speeds up in orbit, it moves to a higher orbit with a larger radius.
If a satellite slows down due to atmospheric drag, it loses energy and drops to a lower, faster orbit.
Space debris in low Earth orbit experiences slight atmospheric drag, causing orbital decay.
Orbital decay leads to re-entry and burning up in the upper atmosphere.

callouts.p: Drag removes energy from a satellite, causing it to descend and speed up, paradoxically.

core.p: Exam questions frequently ask students to compare the features of planetary orbits with comet orbits using specific physical principles.
bullets: Planets have near-circular orbits with low eccentricity; comets have highly elliptical orbits with high eccentricity.
Planets maintain relatively constant speeds; comets experience extreme variations in speed.
Planets orbit within a narrow plane; comets approach the Sun from many different angles and inclinations.
Both are governed by the same laws of gravitation and conservation of energy.

callouts.p: Always use comparative language (e.g., 'higher', 'more elliptical') when contrasting planets and comets.

analogy.t: The Ball on a String and the Tethered Racer
analogy.p:
Imagine spinning a rubber bung on the end of a string in a circle. The tension in the string pulls the bung inward, acting just like gravity. If you let go, the bung flies off in a straight line (inertia). If you pull the string shorter, the bung has to spin faster to keep the tension balanced. 

Where the analogy breaks down: In space, there is no physical string; the invisible force of gravity acts across a vacuum without physical contact. Also, gravity decreases with distance, whereas string tension increases when stretched.

terms.d: The Sun and all celestial bodies bound to it by gravitational forces.
The curved path of a celestial object or spacecraft around a star, planet, or moon.
A stretched circle or oval shape with two focal points.
The time taken for a satellite to complete one full orbit.
The distance from the centre of the orbited body to the orbiting body.
A resultant force towards the centre of a circular path that keeps an object moving in a circle.
The gravitational force per unit mass experienced by a small mass at that point (N/kg).
An artificial satellite with a 24-hour orbital period, staying above the same point on Earth's equator.
The point in an elliptical orbit where a body is closest to the Sun.
The point in an elliptical orbit where a body is furthest from the Sun.
A measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.
The gradual decrease in the radius of a satellite's orbit due to energy loss from atmospheric drag.

mistakes.w: Saying planets orbit in perfect circles.
mistakes.r: Planet orbits are slightly elliptical, not perfect circles.

mistakes.w: Stating that gravity pushes planets away from the Sun.
mistakes.r: Gravity is strictly an attractive force; it pulls objects towards each other.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to add the planet's radius when calculating satellite orbital altitude.
mistakes.r: Orbital radius r must be measured from the centre of the planet, so r = Planet Radius + Altitude.

mistakes.w: Believing comets travel at a constant speed.
mistakes.r: Comets speed up significantly when close to the Sun and slow down when far away.

mistakes.w: Stating that a larger orbit means a higher speed.
mistakes.r: A larger orbit has a weaker gravitational pull, so it requires a slower orbital speed.

mistakes.w: Confusing orbital period with rotational period.
mistakes.r: Orbital period is the time taken to go around the Sun; rotational period is the time taken to spin on its axis (a day).

mistakes.w: Stating that artificial satellites stay up because there is no gravity in space.
mistakes.r: Gravity is strong in space; satellites are in free-fall around Earth while moving fast sideways.

exam.q: Explain why a planet closer to the Sun travels faster than a planet further away.
model: Closer to the Sun, the gravitational field strength is greater
This results in a stronger gravitational force acting on the planet
A stronger force provides a larger centripetal force
Therefore, the planet must travel at a higher speed to maintain a stable circular orbit
exam.tip: Link distance to gravitational field strength, force, and required speed.

exam.q: Calculate the orbital speed of a satellite with an orbital radius of 7.0 x 10^6 m and an orbital period of 5400 seconds. Give your answer to 2 significant figures. (Use pi = 3.14)
model: State equation: v = (2 x pi x r) / T
Substitute values: v = (2 x 3.14 x 7.0 x 10^6) / 5400
Calculate value: v = 8131.48 m/s
Round to 2 sig figs: 8100 m/s
exam.tip: Check your substitution and make sure you round correctly at the final step.

exam.q: Describe the difference between the orbits of planets and the orbits of comets in our solar system.
model: Planet orbits are nearly circular (low eccentricity); comet orbits are highly elliptical (high eccentricity)
Planets maintain relatively constant orbital speeds; comet speeds change dramatically
Planets all orbit in approximately the same plane; comets approach from various inclinations
Planets stay within the inner/outer solar system; comets travel from the inner solar system to the outer edges
exam.tip: Use comparative vocabulary and cover shape, speed, and path.

exam.q: Explain what happens to the kinetic energy of a comet as it moves from aphelion to perihelion.
model: As it moves towards the Sun (perihelion), gravitational potential energy decreases
By conservation of energy, the total energy remains constant
Therefore, kinetic energy increases, so the comet speeds up
exam.tip: Mention conservation of energy and the interchange between GPE and kinetic energy.

exam.q: State the condition necessary for a satellite to remain in a stable circular orbit.
model: The gravitational force must supply the correct centripetal force
The speed and radius must be matched so the radius remains constant
exam.tip: Keep definitions concise and scientifically precise.

exam.q: A satellite's orbit radius is increased. State and explain the effect this has on its orbital speed.
model: Orbital speed decreases
A larger radius means the gravitational force from the central body is weaker
A weaker gravitational force requires a slower speed to maintain a stable circular orbit
exam.tip: Always explain the mechanism via gravitational force strength.

exam.q: Explain why comet tails always point away from the Sun regardless of the comet's direction of travel.
model: Solar wind and radiation pressure push gas and dust away from the Sun
Because the force acts outwards from the Sun, the tail streams in the opposite direction
exam.tip: Recall the dual role of solar wind and radiation pressure.

exam.q: Define a geostationary satellite and state one of its uses.
model: A satellite with an orbital period of exactly 24 hours orbiting above the equator
Used for communications or weather forecasting
exam.tip: Make sure to state both the period and the alignment with the equator.

exam.q: Describe the effect of atmospheric drag on a satellite in low Earth orbit.
model: Drag removes energy from the satellite
The satellite drops to a lower radius and increases in speed
exam.tip: Remember that atmospheric drag causes descent and speeding up.

worked.q: Calculate the orbital speed of the Earth around the Sun, given that the orbital radius is 1.5 x 10^11 m and the orbital period is one year (3.15 x 10^7 seconds). Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
steps: Identify known values: r = 1.5 x 10^11 m, T = 3.15 x 10^7 s
Write down the orbital speed formula: v = (2 x pi x r) / T
Substitute numbers into the formula: v = (2 x 3.1416 x 1.5 x 10^11) / (3.15 x 10^7)
Calculate result: v = 29999.05 m/s
Round to 2 significant figures: 3.0 x 10^4 m/s

worked.q: A communication satellite orbits Earth at an altitude of 3.6 x 10^7 m above Earth's surface. Earth's radius is 6.4 x 10^6 m. Calculate the total orbital radius r and state why the altitude alone cannot be used in the orbital speed formula.
steps: Identify Earth's radius R = 6.4 x 10^6 m and altitude h = 3.6 x 10^7 m
State that orbital radius must be measured from the centre of mass of the planet
Add Earth's radius and altitude: r = R + h = 6.4 x 10^6 + 3.6 x 10^7
Convert numbers to same exponent: 0.64 x 10^7 + 3.6 x 10^7 = 4.24 x 10^7 m
State conclusion: r = 4.2 x 10^7 m (to 2 sig figs)
worked.ans: Orbital radius r = 4.2 x 10^7 m; altitude alone is insufficient because gravitational distance is measured from the centre of the Earth.

phy_ocrb.5.9.summary: These complete Grade 9 revision notes cover the formation of the solar system and the Sun for OCR GCSE Physics B (Twenty First Century Science) triple tier. They explain the gravitational collapse of giant molecular clouds, the conservation of angular momentum leading to protoplanetary discs, accretion processes, and the transition of the protostar into a stable main sequence star through nuclear fusion. The notes feature detailed SVG diagrams, precise definitions, exam traps, and worked examples designed to secure top marks.

core.p: The story of our solar system begins over 4.5 billion years ago within a vast, cold cloud of gas and dust known as a giant molecular cloud or nebula. This cloud consisted mostly of hydrogen and helium, with trace amounts of heavier elements forged by previous generations of stars. Under specific conditions, external triggers such as a nearby supernova shockwave caused local regions of the cloud to increase in density, setting off a chain reaction of gravitational collapse.
bullets: Nebulae are giant interstellar clouds composed largely of hydrogen gas and helium gas.
Interstellar dust grains, including silicates and carbon compounds, make up a small percentage of the cloud's mass.
Random thermal motions and weak magnetic fields initially oppose the inward pull of gravity.
Gravitational potential energy is continuously converted into thermal energy as the cloud contracts.

callouts.p: A giant cloud of dust and gas in space, primarily composed of hydrogen and helium, which serves as the birthplace for stars and planetary systems.

core.p: When a region of the molecular cloud exceeds a critical mass limit known as the Jeans mass, the inward gravitational force overwhelms the outward thermal pressure exerted by the gas. The gas particles accelerate inwards towards the center of mass in a process called free-fall collapse. As the material rushes inward, gravitational potential energy is released and converted into internal kinetic energy, causing the core region to heat up significantly.
bullets: Gravity pulls all surrounding matter toward a common center of mass.
Thermal pressure from particle collisions initially tries to push outward, but is insufficient once gravitational dominance is established.
The collapsing core becomes increasingly dense and opaque, trapping the thermal energy inside.
The temperature at the center rises sharply as the collapse proceeds.

callouts.p: During gravitational collapse, gravitational potential energy is converted into kinetic energy and thermal energy, causing the temperature of the collapsing core to skyrocket.

fig.cap: Gravitational collapse of an interstellar gas cloud into a dense central core due to gravity exceeding thermal pressure.

core.p: Because the original molecular cloud possessed a very small initial net rotation, conservation of angular momentum plays a crucial role during its collapse. As the cloud shrinks in radius, it must spin faster to conserve its total angular momentum (L = mvr). This increasing rotational speed generates centrifugal effects perpendicular to the spin axis, causing the spherical cloud to flatten out into a rotating protoplanetary disc.
bullets: Angular momentum must be conserved in an isolated rotating system.
As radius r decreases, rotational velocity v must increase significantly.
Material along the rotational axis collapses more easily than material in the equatorial plane.
The resulting flattened structure is known as the protoplanetary or solar nebula disc.

callouts.p: Students often think the cloud collapses into a flat disc because of gravity alone. Gravity pulls inward in all directions; the flattening is specifically caused by the conservation of angular momentum and centrifugal effects in the plane perpendicular to the axis of rotation.

core.p: At the very center of the collapsing, spinning nebula, the densest concentration of matter forms a protostar. This central object is not yet a true star because its core is not hot enough or dense enough to initiate nuclear fusion. Instead, the protostar shines purely from the immense thermal energy generated by its ongoing gravitational contraction and the continuous accretion of infalling matter from the surrounding disc.
bullets: The protostar is the precursor stage to a main sequence star.
Energy radiation is powered entirely by Kelvin-Helmholtz contraction (gravitational energy release).
Infalling gas and dust continue to feed mass onto the growing protostar.
Winds and bipolar outflows begin to clear away the surrounding envelope of gas.

callouts.p: A very young star that is still gathering mass from its parent molecular cloud, powered by gravitational contraction rather than nuclear fusion.

core.p: Surrounding the central protostar, the flattened protoplanetary disc contains the building blocks of future planets. Within this disc, microscopic dust grains collide and stick together through electrostatic and mechanical forces in a process called accretion. Over millions of years, these tiny grains grow into larger millimeter-sized pebbles, then kilometer-sized planetesimals, and eventually protoplanets through continuous gravitational attraction and gentle collisions.
bullets: Accretion is the gradual accumulation of matter through microscopic and macroscopic collisions.
Planetesimals are solid bodies ranging from hundreds of meters to kilometers in diameter.
Protoplanets grow via runaway accretion, sweeping up surrounding planetesimals in their orbital paths.
Turbulence and gas drag within the disc help concentrate solid particles into denser midplane layers.

callouts.p: Planets form through bottom-up accretion: dust grains stick together to form pebbles, pebbles form planetesimals, planetesimals form protoplanets, and protoplanets form full planets.

core.p: The temperature across the protoplanetary disc was not uniform; it was extremely hot near the central protostar and much colder further out. This temperature gradient dictated what type of materials could condense out of the gas phase. Within the frost line (close to the Sun), temperatures were too high for volatile compounds to condense, leaving behind only rocky, metallic materials. Beyond the frost line, volatile ices (water, ammonia, methane) remained solid, allowing massive gas and ice giant planets to form.
bullets: The frost line (or snow line) marks the boundary where water vapor condenses into solid ice grains.
Inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) formed from rocky and metallic materials.
Outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) formed from a massive core of ice and rock surrounded by accreted hydrogen and helium gas.
Asteroids and comets represent leftover planetesimals that never merged into larger planets.

callouts.p: The distance from the central protostar in a protoplanetary disc beyond which volatile substances such as water, ammonia, and methane could condense into solid ice grains.

core.p: As the young Sun matured, it entered a phase of heightened activity characterized by strong stellar winds and intense high-energy radiation (the T Tauri phase). This powerful solar wind, combined with intense radiation pressure, swept away the remaining primordial gas and dust from the protoplanetary disc into interstellar space. This clearing process abruptly ended the growth phase of the gas giant planets, locking in the mass and architecture of the solar system roughly 50 million years after its initial formation.
bullets: T Tauri stars exhibit extremely vigorous stellar winds and magnetic outflows.
Radiation pressure exerts a subtle outward force on dust and gas particles.
Leftover hydrogen and helium gas was blown out beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Planetary growth halted once the raw materials were cleared away.

callouts.p: Make sure you can link the clearing of the nebula to the action of the early solar wind and radiation pressure from the young Sun.

core.h: 8. Ignition of Nuclear Fusion in the Sun
core.p: While the planets were slowly accreting in the disc, the central protostar continued its relentless gravitational contraction. As more mass fell inward, the core temperature and pressure climbed to unimaginable heights. When the core temperature finally reached approximately 10 million degrees Celsius (10 MK), nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium ignited. This monumental event marked the birth of the Sun as a true main sequence star.
bullets: Core temperature reached approximately 10 million Kelvin.
Protons (hydrogen nuclei) overcome their electrostatic repulsion via high thermal kinetic energy.
Nuclear fusion converts hydrogen into helium, releasing immense amounts of energy according to E = mc^2.
Radiation and thermal pressure created by fusion balance the inward pull of gravity.

callouts.p: A protostar officially becomes a star (entering the main sequence) the exact moment sustained nuclear fusion of hydrogen begins in its core.

core.p: Once the Sun ignited its nuclear fusion engine, it entered a stable state known as hydrostatic equilibrium. In this state, two opposing forces are balanced perfectly throughout the star: the inward gravitational force pulling all the mass toward the center, and the outward thermal and radiation pressure generated by nuclear fusion reactions in the core. This delicate balance allows the Sun to shine stably for billions of years.
bullets: Inward force = Gravitational attraction.
Outward force = Thermal pressure + radiation pressure from core fusion.
If fusion rate drops, the core contracts, heats up, and fusion increases.
If fusion rate rises, the core expands, cools, and fusion decreases.

callouts.p: The stable condition in a star where the inward force of gravity is exactly balanced by the outward thermal and radiation pressure from nuclear fusion.

core.p: The specific nuclear fusion process powering the Sun is called the proton-proton (p-p) chain. In this multi-step reaction, four hydrogen nuclei (protons) are fused together to form one nucleus of helium-4, accompanied by the release of two positrons, two neutrinos, and gamma-ray photons. A tiny fraction of the initial mass is converted directly into energy during this fusion sequence, providing the power that illuminates the solar system.
bullets: Step 1: Two protons fuse to form deuterium, a positron, and a neutrino.
Step 2: A proton fuses with deuterium to form helium-3 and a gamma-ray photon.
Step 3: Two helium-3 nuclei fuse to form helium-4, releasing two excess protons.
Mass defect: The combined mass of the final helium-4 nucleus is less than the four original protons, with the missing mass converted into energy.

callouts.p: Four hydrogen nuclei fuse into one helium-4 nucleus, releasing energy via E = mc^2 due to a small mass defect.

analogy.p: Imagine a chef making pizza dough. The chef takes a ball of dough (representing the giant molecular cloud) and tosses it into the air while spinning it. As the dough spins and is pulled inward by the chef's hands (gravity), it flattens out into a wide, rotating disc. At the very center, the thickest part remains as the dough ball (the protostar), while the flat outer disc represents the protoplanetary disc where ingredients (planets) gather. This analogy breaks down because pizza dough flattens due to mechanical stretching and elasticity, whereas the solar nebula flattens due to conservation of angular momentum and centrifugal effects during gravitational collapse.

terms.d: The process by which celestial bodies grow in size through the gradual collision and sticking together of dust grains and planetesimals.

A massive, cold interstellar cloud of gas and dust from which stars and planetary systems form.
The physical state in which the inward gravitational force acting on a star is exactly balanced by the outward thermal and radiation pressure.
The critical mass threshold that a gas cloud must exceed for its self-gravity to overcome internal thermal pressure and trigger gravitational collapse.
The stable stage in a star's life cycle where it fuses hydrogen into helium in its core and remains in hydrostatic equilibrium.
An interstellar cloud of gas (mainly hydrogen and helium) and dust particles in space.
A solid object formed from dust grains in a protoplanetary disc, ranging from meters to kilometers in size, acting as a building block for planets.
A rotating disc of dense gas and dust surrounding a newly formed protostar, out of which planets eventually form.
An early stage in stellar evolution where a collapsing cloud of gas is heated by gravitational contraction before nuclear fusion begins.
The primary nuclear fusion reaction sequence by which low-mass stars like the Sun convert hydrogen into helium.
An early stage in a low-mass star's life characterized by strong stellar winds and high magnetic activity that clears the surrounding nebula.

mistakes.w: Saying gravity causes the protoplanetary disc to flatten.
mistakes.r: Gravity pulls inward in all directions equally; the flattening is caused by the conservation of angular momentum and centrifugal forces perpendicular to the rotational axis.

mistakes.w: Stating that a protostar is powered by nuclear fusion.
mistakes.r: A protostar is powered entirely by gravitational potential energy converted into thermal energy through contraction, not fusion.

mistakes.w: Claiming planets formed from gas clouds condensing directly into planets.
mistakes.r: Planets formed through bottom-up accretion: dust grains stuck together to form planetesimals, which then coalesced into protoplanets.

mistakes.w: Stating that all planets formed from the same materials regardless of distance.
mistakes.r: Temperature gradients in the disc created a frost line; inner planets are rocky/metallic, while outer planets are gas/ice giants.

mistakes.w: Confusing the main sequence with the protostar stage.
mistakes.r: The main sequence begins only when nuclear fusion ignites in the core; protostars have no core fusion.

mistakes.w: Believing the solar wind compressed the nebula to form stars.
mistakes.r: External triggers like supernova shockwaves or cloud collisions triggered compression, whereas solar winds cleared the nebula away later.

mistakes.w: Forgetting that angular momentum is conserved as the cloud contracts.
mistakes.r: As the radius decreases, the rotational speed must increase (L = mvr) to conserve angular momentum.

exam.q: Describe how a giant molecular cloud begins to form a star and its planetary system.
model: A region of the molecular cloud exceeds the Jeans mass.
Inward gravitational force exceeds outward thermal pressure.
The cloud undergoes gravitational collapse.
Gravitational potential energy is converted into thermal energy, forming a hot core (protostar).
exam.tip: Mention the balance between gravity and thermal pressure, and the energy conversion.

exam.q: Explain why the collapsing cloud of gas and dust flattened into a rotating disc.
model: The original cloud had a small net rotation.
As the cloud contracted in radius, its rotational speed increased.
This happened due to the conservation of angular momentum, leading to centrifugal effects that flattened the structure into a disc.
exam.tip: Always link flattening to the conservation of angular momentum.

exam.q: State what powers a protostar before nuclear fusion begins.
model: Gravitational contraction / gravitational potential energy converting to thermal energy.
exam.tip: Do not mention nuclear fusion for protostars.

exam.q: Explain the difference in composition between the inner terrestrial planets and the outer gas giant planets.
model: There was a temperature gradient across the protoplanetary disc.
Inside the frost line, it was too hot for volatile substances to condense, leaving only rocky and metallic materials to form terrestrial planets.
Beyond the frost line, water and other volatiles froze into solid ice grains.
This allowed massive cores to form, attracting large envelopes of hydrogen and helium gas to form gas giants.
exam.tip: Reference the frost line and temperature differences.

exam.q: Define hydrostatic equilibrium in the context of the Sun.
model: The inward force of gravity is balanced by...
...the outward thermal and radiation pressure from nuclear fusion in the core.
exam.tip: You must mention both opposing forces for the full 2 marks.

exam.q: Name the nuclear fusion process that powers the Sun and state what is converted into what.
model: Proton-proton chain.
Hydrogen nuclei (protons) are converted into helium nuclei.
A small amount of mass is lost (mass defect) and converted into energy.
exam.tip: State both the reactants/products and the mass-energy conversion.

exam.q: Explain what event marked the birth of the Sun as a main sequence star.
model: The core temperature reached approximately 10 million Kelvin.
Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium ignited in the core.
exam.tip: Focus on the ignition of core fusion.

exam.q: Describe how the remaining gas and dust in the protoplanetary disc were cleared away.
model: Strong stellar winds from the young Sun (T Tauri phase)...
...combined with radiation pressure, blew the remaining gas and dust out into interstellar space.
exam.tip: Include both stellar wind and radiation pressure.

exam.q: Explain what planetesimals are and how they contributed to planet formation.
model: Planetesimals are solid bodies ranging from meters to kilometers in size formed from dust accretion.
They collided and stuck together through gravitational attraction...
...forming protoplanets and eventually full planets.
exam.tip: Trace the step from dust grains to planetesimals to planets.

worked.q: A gas cloud collapses from an initial radius of 1.0 x 10^15 m to a final radius of 1.0 x 10^11 m. If its initial rotational speed was 1.0 x 10^-6 rad/s, estimate its final rotational speed assuming angular momentum is conserved and mass distribution remains proportional.
steps: State the principle of conservation of angular momentum: L = I * omega = constant.
For a uniform sphere/disc approximation where I is proportional to m * r^2, m_1 * r_1^2 * omega_1 = m_2 * r_2^2 * omega_2.
Since mass m is constant, r_1^2 * omega_1 = r_2^2 * omega_2.
Rearrange for final angular speed omega_2 = omega_1 * (r_1 / r_2)^2.

worked.q: A protostar radiates energy at a rate of 2.0 x 10^28 W entirely due to gravitational potential energy release. If its mass is 2.0 x 10^30 kg and average radius is 7.0 x 10^8 m, estimate the gravitational potential energy released (using U = G*M^2 / R where G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2) and calculate the approximate free-fall timescale if it radiates at this constant rate.
steps: Calculate gravitational potential energy U = (6.67 x 10^-11 * (2.0 x 10^30)^2) / (7.0 x 10^8).
Calculate time t = U / Power = (3.81 x 10^41 J) / (2.0 x 10^28 W).
t = 1.905 x 10^13 seconds.
Convert seconds to years: t = 1.905 x 10^13 / (3.15 x 10^7 s/year) = ~604,000 years.
